analysis.one_liner: Ends job protections for new federal hires, letting agencies fire them without notice or appeal.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have put new federal employees on at-will status, capped their raises, and curtailed union rights, died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how the federal government employs its roughly two million civilian workers. Starting a year after passage, new federal hires could be removed or suspended by their agency head "for good cause, bad cause, or no cause at all," without notice or the right to appeal [S2][S3]. Employees could suspend workers first and answer questions later, appeal an adverse action to only one agency, and lose any pay raise unless they scored a 4 or 5 out of 5 on their latest review [S2][S3]. It would also end paid "official time" for union representatives and bar employees from using any government property for union business [S2][S3], and require forfeiting a federal pension after a felony conviction related to the job [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and never moved again before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Agency heads and federal managers would gain sweeping power to hire and fire at will, and to suspend employees immediately with the burden of appeal falling on the worker. Anti-union interests would benefit from ending paid union representation time and restricting union activity on government property. Supporters argued it would make the civil service more accountable and easier to manage [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Starting one year after enactment, every new civil-service hire could be removed or suspended by the agency head for good cause, bad cause, or no cause at all, without notice or right of appeal [S2][S3].

Agencies could suspend employees for misconduct or poor performance first, with notice and a chance to answer only afterward, and the Merit Systems Protection Board could not reinstate the worker until the appeal concluded; in cases of "critical necessity" the agency could immediately replace the worker [S3].
Employees could appeal an adverse personnel action to only one agency, cutting off parallel routes to the Merit Systems Protection Board, the Office of Special Counsel, or the EEOC [S2][S3].
No employee scoring below 4 out of 5 on a performance review could receive a pay raise, and a union grievance that upgraded a rating could not produce a raise [S2][S3].
The bill eliminated official time for union bargaining representatives and prohibited using government property, including office space or computers, for internal union business [S2][S3].
Federal employees would forfeit their pension if finally convicted of a felony committed during service or, after separation, a felony related to their former government position [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal employees, most directly new hires after the bill's effective date, would bear the cost: the near-total loss of due process before firing or suspension, tighter limits on appealing, and pay raises blocked by a single subpar performance review. Federal employee unions would lose paid representation time and the ability to use any government resources for internal union business. Existing employees would keep formal protections, but any wrongdoing could mean forfeiting their earned pension [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal workers, unions, and new hires

drawbacks.text: At-will firing without notice or appeal removes the basic due process that has governed federal employment for over a century, exposing workers to removal for arbitrary or politically motivated reasons; the bill's own oversight standards rely on agency self-policing rather than independent review [S3].

Linking all pay raises to a 4-out-of-5 performance score, and barring court- or grievance-won rating upgrades from producing raises, could penalize solid performers and invite rating inflation rather than honest appraisals [S3].
Ending official time would force unions to fund representation entirely on their own dime, weakening the negotiation process that governs pay and conditions for the whole federal workforce [S2][S3].

Limiting each worker to a single appeal route could leave discrimination or whistleblower claims without a full hearing, even though the bill preserved the underlying discrimination and whistleblower statutes on paper [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — faster removal of genuinely underperforming or corrupt employees, and pension forfeiture for felons — has some legitimate appeal. But the bill's mechanism is a sledgehammer: it trades a universal, century-old system of notice, cause, and appeal for manager discretion with no independent check until after the punishment, and it couples that with broad restrictions on union activity that go well beyond any efficiency rationale. An honest supporter would have to concede that the at-will and single-appeal provisions do far more to strip worker protections than to fix bad-employee removals, which agencies can already pursue through existing procedures.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight Committee the day it was introduced, and the Congress ended without the committee ever acting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Todd Rokita (R-IN) introduced the bill on September 28, 2016, near the end of the 114th Congress, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform [S1][S5].
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, one House Republican [S4].
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal employees and their unions came out ahead: by dying quietly in committee, the bill left the existing civil service system of for-cause removal, appeal rights, and paid union representation fully intact for another Congress.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Federal employee unions
against.what_they_did: Would have lost official time, resource use, and grievance-based pay upgrades under the bill; their opposition contributed to the political environment in which it died

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporters on record were two Republicans, and it died in committee with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate paid official time for union representatives and ban using government property for internal union business, sharply weakening federal-sector unions' capacity to represent workers. Union representation also mediates workplace disputes that affect the quality of public services, so the loss cuts both ways for the public.

Managers would gain authority to fire or suspend at will, with no notice, no appeal, and the ability to immediately replace suspended workers. That concentration of power is exercised over employees' livelihoods with limited external check.
